opus-5.5.text:
I think the people who adapt fastest are the ones who were never too attached to the old way of working. In the pre-training era, a lot of the craft was data: cleaning it, mixing it, scaling it, and waiting weeks to see a loss curve. You could be very good at that and still treat the model as something you feed rather than something you interact with.

With RL and inference-time scaling, the feedback loop feels completely different. You're designing environments, reward signals, and verification, and then watching how the model actually behaves, how it reasons, where it hacks the reward, where it gives up too early. People who enjoy that kind of close observation, almost like debugging a living system, tend to feel at home very quickly. They look at the trajectories themselves instead of just staring at aggregate metrics.

I've also noticed that people with strong engineering instincts adapt well, because RL infrastructure is genuinely hard. Rollouts, asynchronous training, long contexts, keeping everything stable at scale. A lot of research progress here is really unblocked by infrastructure. So someone who can move between "what should the reward be" and "why is this pipeline stalling" is extremely valuable.

The hardest part, honestly, is mindset. In RL there's much less certainty. Things that worked last month might stop working, and results can be noisy. People who need a clean, predictable recipe can find it frustrating at first. The ones who thrive are comfortable with ambiguity and treat each failure as information. They're curious rather than anxious.

And younger researchers often have an advantage, not because they know more, but because they have fewer assumptions to unlearn. They just ask, "What happens if we let the model think longer?" and try it. That openness matters a lot right now, because the field is moving so fast that experience can sometimes become a kind of baggage.

r001.rationale: The response says some people feel at home quickly because they are open to the new paradigm, but it does not suggest they feel no real adaptation occurred.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's worth separating two kinds of people here, because the adaptation looks very different depending on where you're coming from.

The first group is people who grew up, so to speak, in the pretraining era. Their intuition is built around data scaling, loss curves, architecture tweaks. For them, the RL paradigm feels uncomfortable at first because the feedback loop is so different. In pretraining, you change something, you watch the loss go down, and you more or less trust that downstream capability follows. In RL, the signal is much noisier and much more delayed. You can run an experiment for a week and still not be sure whether the model actually learned to reason or just learned to game the reward. So the people who adapt well from this group are the ones who are willing to give up some of that comfort, and become almost obsessive about evaluation and about reading the model's actual outputs, not just the curves.

The second group is people who naturally think in terms of environments and objectives. Some of them came from classical RL, game playing, robotics, or even from systems or math backgrounds. For them the paradigm feels almost obvious. The hard part for them is the opposite: they underestimate how much the base model matters. They want to jump straight to reward design and clever algorithms, and they have to learn that if the pretraining is weak, no amount of RL will pull the capability out. So their adaptation is really about learning humility toward the foundation.

What I notice across both groups is that the people who thrive share a certain temperament. They are patient with ambiguity. They are comfortable with the idea that the model will surprise them, sometimes in good ways and sometimes in bad ways, and they treat that as information rather than as a failure. And they tend to be very hands-on. In this paradigm you cannot delegate the understanding of the model to a dashboard. You have to sit with the rollouts, see where the reasoning breaks, and form a hypothesis about why.

There's also an emotional dimension that I think people underestimate. The pace of progress in RL inference has been so fast that even people who are well suited to it feel a kind of constant pressure, because what worked three months ago may be irrelevant now. The ones who adapt best are not necessarily the smartest, but the ones who can keep updating without becoming cynical or exhausted. They stay curious. I think that's actually the biggest predictor.

r001.rationale: The response describes adaptation as different for two groups and says some find the paradigm almost obvious, but it does not suggest that adaptable people feel they underwent no real adaptation.

astra-6.text:
I think people who are suited to it often find the transition quite natural. They’re comfortable with uncertainty, and they enjoy learning through experimentation: forming a hypothesis, running something, looking at the results, and revising their understanding.

But there’s still an adjustment. With reinforcement learning, improving the training objective doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve improved the behavior you actually care about. You have to keep asking whether the reward and the evaluation capture what you intended. And when you bring inference into that picture, you also have to think about how effectively the model uses additional computation.

So I’d say the key is being willing to let experiments challenge your intuition. People who enjoy that process tend to adapt well.

r001.rationale: The response says the transition often feels natural, but also describes an adjustment; it does not clearly suggest people feel they underwent no real adaptation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people who are well suited to this paradigm find the transition quite natural. They’re comfortable with uncertainty and with learning through experimentation. Rather than expecting an idea to work immediately, they form a hypothesis, run an experiment, look at the feedback, and adjust.

But there’s still an adaptation process. With reinforcement learning, you have to think carefully about what you’re rewarding and whether that reward actually reflects the behavior you want. And at inference time, you’re thinking about how to use additional computation effectively. So the shift is partly technical, but it’s also a change in mindset: becoming comfortable with an iterative process where the results can surprise you.

r001.rationale: The response says the transition feels quite natural for people suited to the paradigm, but also explicitly describes an adaptation process and a shift in mindset. It does not suggest they undergo no real adaptation.
